673.title: Be a renunciant at home
673.hook: re man aiso kar sanniaasaa: make your home your forest, your heart your hermitage (Dasam, Ramkali Patshahi 10)
673.howItsDone: Sikhs sing re man aiso kar sanniaasaa in kirtan as a picture of the householder's path: detachment and devotion lived inside family and work.

segments.voice: Yesterday, subh karman, the good deeds never to turn from, and your line: never turn from good. Today, the Tenth Guru again, this time on where a spiritual life is lived.

It's an old fantasy: quit the job, sell the stuff, move to a cabin in the mountains, and finally become the calm, deep person ordinary life never leaves time for. In India, that dream has an old and honored form: the sannyasi, the renunciant who leaves home for the forest, with matted hair and ashes on the skin. Guru Gobind Singh wrote a shabad that takes every piece of that picture, one by one, and moves it indoors.
screen: `THE CABIN IN THE MOUNTAINS.` → `THE SANNYASI IN THE FOREST.` → `EVERY PIECE MOVED INDOORS.`

segments.voice: The shabad is in Raag Ramkali, among the Tenth Guru's hymns in the Dasam Granth. It opens: re man aiso kar sanniaasaa. In paraphrase: O mind, practice renunciation like this. Think of your whole house as the forest, and stay detached inside your own heart. Then it goes through the renunciant's kit, item by item, giving each a new meaning. Make self-control your matted hair. Make union with God your daily bath. Let your teacher be wisdom, and smear the Name on yourself like ashes. Eat little, sleep little, love mercy and forgiveness. Keep a gentle, contented nature, and keep lust, anger, pride, greed and attachment out of the mind. It's a clever move. The shabad doesn't mock the renunciant. It takes the forest life seriously, then says the real forest is a way of living, and you can carry it into a kitchen. That's a deep thread in Sikh teaching, running back to Guru Nanak, who lived as a householder and taught that God is found in the middle of ordinary life, not by escaping it. The word for the inner detachment here is udaas: unattached, free inside. You can be udaas in a crowded house, and caught in a quiet cave. So the question isn't where you live. It's whether, in the middle of the noise, there's a small clearing inside you where the Name is remembered.
screen: `O MIND, RENOUNCE LIKE THIS.` · `YOUR HOUSE IS THE FOREST.` · `THE KIT, GIVEN NEW MEANING.` · `A CLEARING IN A FULL HOUSE.` · then, large: `THE FOREST AT HOME.`

segments.voice: Stay exactly where you are, without tidying anything, and let the room be the forest: hear its sounds, the fridge, traffic, someone in the next room, as if they were birds and wind. Sit as still as a hermit would, feet rooted. If you pray, say Waheguru in the clearing you've made.
Udaas, unattached, free inside: the Tenth Guru's shabad says think of your house as the forest, stay udaas within, and wear self-control, mercy and the Name as the hermit's marks.
Your line: the forest at home. A clearing inside, even in a full house. That's day six hundred seventy-three.

674.title: Songs of mourning
674.hook: Guru Nanak's dirges are sung for the dead, remembering that all must go (Vadhans M1, ang 578)
674.howItsDone: At Sikh funerals and in the days after, families gather for kirtan, Kirtan Sohila and Ardas, and Guru Nanak's alaahneeaa are among the hymns sung, in place of the old custom of ritual wailing.

segments.voice: Yesterday, udaas, free inside, and your line: the forest at home. This part of the path has sung for weddings and births. Today it sings at the other turning point.

In old Punjab, when someone died, the women of the village gathered in the courtyard. They sat in a circle and wailed, a lament with a rhythm to it, one woman leading, the others answering, beating their chests. The custom was called siapa, and the lament songs were alaahnees. Grief was loud, public, and shaped by tradition. Guru Nanak knew those songs. And he did something unexpected with them: he wrote his own.
screen: `WOMEN GATHERED IN A COURTYARD.` → `A LAMENT WITH A RHYTHM.` → `GURU NANAK WROTE HIS OWN.`

segments.voice: Guru Nanak's alaahneeaa, his laments, are in Raag Vadhans, starting on Ang five seventy-eight. He kept the form people knew, but changed what it sang about. The first begins, in paraphrase: blessed is the Creator, the true King, who has set the whole world to its tasks. When the measure of a life is full, the soul is taken, and loved ones cry out. The body and soul are parted when the days are done. Notice the first word. A mourning song that opens with blessed. It doesn't deny the grief; the hymn says plainly that the family weeps. But it sets the grief inside something larger: a Creator who gives each life its span. Then the truth that runs through these songs: everyone who comes must go. It isn't said to scold anyone for crying. It's said the way a friend at a funeral says, gently, this is the road we all walk. Sikh practice took this to heart: the Sikh code of conduct discourages loud wailing at a death. Kirtan is sung, often Kirtan Sohila, the bedtime prayer, and the Ardas is said. A reading of the Guru Granth Sahib is often begun in the days after, and the alaahneeaa are among the hymns sung. Grief is allowed. But it's held in praise, and in the plain, shared knowledge that this is how every life goes.

segments.voice: Bring to mind someone who has died, a grandparent, a friend, even a pet, and let an ordinary memory come rather than the hardest one: their laugh, a meal, a phrase they used. Let any sadness be there too, and quietly give thanks for the days they were given. If you pray, say Waheguru for them.
Alaahnee. A lament, the old Punjabi mourning song. Guru Nanak's alaahneeaa keep its form but open with praise, and remember that everyone who comes must go.
Your line: all must go. Grief is allowed here, and it is held in praise. Until tomorrow.

675.title: The death of the brave
675.hook: death is the right of the brave, if it is accepted in the Lord's court (Vadhans M1, ang 579)
675.howItsDone: Sikhs sing Guru Nanak's alaahneeaa at funerals and remembrances, and these lines on the death of the brave are often recalled when martyrs are remembered.

segments.voice: Yesterday, the alaahnee, the lament that opens with praise, and your line: all must go. Today, the next lament asks a harder question: if all must go, how?

People who work in hospice sometimes say the same thing: there's a difference between someone who dies afraid and someone who dies ready. Not braver in the movie sense. Just settled. They've said what they needed to say. They've made their peace. Most of us don't like to think about it at all. We change the subject, knock on wood, scroll past. Guru Nanak's second lament doesn't change the subject. It says there's such a thing as a good death, and it says who gets one.
screen: `DYING AFRAID, OR DYING READY.` → `WE CHANGE THE SUBJECT.` → `A LAMENT THAT DOESN'T.`

segments.voice: The second of Guru Nanak's alaahneeaa, on Ang five seventy-nine, has a line Sikhs know well. In paraphrase: death is the right of the brave, of true heroes, if their death is accepted. And nearby: don't call death bad, people, if one knows how to truly die. The word for the brave is sooraa, a hero, a warrior. But look who the hymn says the heroes are: they alone are called brave who receive honor in the true court. They leave with honor, and are honored when they arrive. So bravery here isn't measured by the battlefield. It's measured by acceptance in the dargah, the Lord's court. What makes a death accepted? The hymn's answer, and the Granth's answer everywhere, is a life lived remembering the Name, serving, honest. The death of the brave is the end of a brave life, one that didn't flinch from truth. That's why these lines mean so much to a community with many martyrs. Sikhs remember Guru Arjan, Guru Tegh Bahadur, the Tenth Guru's sons, and countless others who faced death without giving up their faith. But the hymn belongs just as much to a grandmother dying in her bed, having lived kindly and remembered God. Her death, too, is the death of the brave. One more word: parvaan, accepted, approved, signed off. It's the key to the line. The question isn't how you die. It's whether the life it ends is accepted.

segments.voice: Think of the next hour of your day, and what it would look like lived bravely in this hymn's sense: not dramatic, just true, the honest answer, the patient word, the thing you've been avoiding. Choose one, and picture yourself doing it calmly. If you pray, say Waheguru, and ask to live this hour in a way that would be accepted.

Your line: accepted in his court. Bravery is measured by how a life is lived. Six hundred seventy-five days in.

676.title: A shabad for your home
676.hook: many families have a shabad they keep for their house
676.howItsDone: Some Sikh families keep a favorite shabad for their home: framed by the door, sung at bedtime or on family occasions, often first heard at a house blessing with Sukhmani Sahib and Ardas.

segments.voice: Yesterday, sooraa, the brave who are honored in the true court, and your line: accepted in his court. We've sung through weddings and funerals. Today the shabads come home, to an ordinary house on an ordinary day.

In some Sikh homes, the shabad is on the wall before anyone sings it: a framed line of Gurmukhi by the front door, or above the stove, or in the hallway. Ask about it, and you'll often get a story. It was my grandmother's favorite. My dad sang it when we moved from Kenya. We played it the night the baby came home. Families have songs the way they have recipes, passed down without anyone deciding to. In some Sikh households, one of those songs is a shabad.
screen: `A FRAMED LINE BY THE DOOR.` → `EVERY LINE HAS A STORY.` → `SONGS PASSED DOWN LIKE RECIPES.`

segments.voice: Shabad means word, and in Sikh life it means a hymn of the Guru Granth Sahib, the Word sung. There's no rule that a family must have one shabad of its own. But some do, and it happens in ordinary ways. A house is blessed with a reading of Sukhmani Sahib and an Ardas when a family moves in, and one line from that day sticks. A grandmother hums the same hymn every evening for years, and her grandchildren hum it without knowing the words. A parent sings one to a child at bedtime, and it becomes theirs. Some keep a well-loved line like dukh bhanjan teraa naam: Your Name destroys pain. That shabad of Guru Arjan, on Ang two eighteen, goes on: dwell on it through all the hours of the day; this is the perfect True Guru's wisdom. Others choose taatee vaao na lagaee, the hot wind that doesn't touch, or the Anand Sahib's opening joy. Why does it matter? A household shabad works like a family's memory. It's there at the birthday and at the hospital, sung in the car and over the dishes. When something hard happens, nobody has to search for words. The words are already in the house, worn smooth by use. And underneath is a Sikh idea: the Guru isn't kept only in the gurdwara. The Word can live where you live, in the kitchen and the hallway, sung by people in their socks.

segments.voice: Think back over the lines you've met on this path, a line from the laavan, the hot wind, the Name that ends pain, and ask which one you'd want in your house: by the door, at bedtime, on a hard day. Let one rise, and say its words or its meaning silently, as if in your own kitchen. If you pray, say Waheguru after it.

677.title: How ragis choose
677.hook: the singers choose shabads for the hour, the season and the occasion
677.howItsDone: In gurdwaras, ragi jathas sing kirtan through the day, choosing shabads by raag, hour, season and occasion, such as Asa di Var at dawn and the laavan at weddings.

segments.voice: Yesterday, dukh bhanjan, the Name that ends pain, and your line: our shabad. Today, the people who choose the shabads for everyone else.

A good DJ reads the room: slow songs late, upbeat ones when people walk in, nothing sad at a birthday. A ragi does something like that, with far older rules and far higher stakes. Sit in a gurdwara at four in the morning, at noon, and at sunset, and you'll hear different music each time. Go on a wedding day and on the day of a funeral, and the shabads change again. Someone is choosing.
screen: `A DJ READS THE ROOM.` → `DAWN, NOON, SUNSET SOUND DIFFERENT.` → `SOMEONE IS CHOOSING.`

segments.voice: A ragi is a singer of kirtan, Gurbani set to music. The word comes from raag, the melodic framework of Indian classical music. Ragis often sing in a small group, a jatha, with harmoniums and a tabla. Behind them stretches a long line: Sikh tradition remembers Bhai Mardana playing the rabab beside Guru Nanak, and the Gurus kept musicians at their courts. The Guru Granth Sahib itself is arranged by raag: after the opening prayers, its hymns are grouped from Sri Raag to Jaijavanti. Each raag has a mood, and in the Indian tradition, many have a time of day or a season. So a ragi chooses on three levels. The hour: at dawn, gurdwaras often sing Asa di Var in Raag Asa; in the evening, other raags and the Rehras. The season: Basant, the spring raag, is sung in its season, and Malhar, the raag of rain, comes into its own in the monsoon. And the occasion: the laavan in Raag Suhi for a wedding, the alaahneeaa in Vadhans for mourning, a shabad of comfort when the sangat is grieving. Then there's the moment itself. A good ragi listens to the room, to the news of the week, to who's sitting there. That's the real skill: not only singing beautifully, but knowing which Word this sangat needs to hear today. Sikhs say the Guru speaks through the shabad. The ragi's choice is how it arrives at the right time.

678.title: Learning one by heart
678.hook: learning one shabad by heart means it's there when you need it
678.howItsDone: Sikhs often learn their daily prayers and favorite shabads by heart, often as children repeating after a parent or grandparent, so they can recite them anywhere.

segments.voice: Yesterday, the ragi, who chooses the right shabad for the hour, and your line: the right song. A ragi knows hundreds of shabads. Today, the gift of knowing just one.

Phone numbers used to live in people's heads. Now they live in phones, and mostly that's fine, until the battery dies at the wrong moment. The same is true of words that steady us. A line saved in an app is no help in an MRI machine, or at three in the morning, or in the half second before you say something you'll regret. Only what's inside you is there then.
screen: `PHONE NUMBERS WE USED TO KNOW.` → `MEMORY HANDED TO OUR POCKETS.` → `ONLY WHAT'S INSIDE IS THERE.`

segments.voice: In Punjabi, to learn something by heart is to make it kanth, literally, to put it in the throat. It's a lovely image: the words live where your voice comes from, ready to rise. Before printed books, a handwritten copy of the scripture was a precious thing, and Sikh tradition remembers Gurbani carried kanth, in memory. Children learned the Japji Sahib by repeating it after a grandparent each morning. Sikhs who keep Nitnem often know their daily prayers by heart, the Nitnem you've met this year: Japji, Jaap, the Savaiye, Chaupai, Anand, Rehras, Sohila. Some know long hymns like Sukhmani Sahib. And the Granth itself treats the Word as something held inside. Guru Amar Das says, on Ang sixty-seven, in paraphrase: the Guru's bani is the light in this world; by grace it comes to dwell in the mind. That's the hope: not words you look up, but words that live in you. Learning by heart changes how a shabad works. Read on a page, it's information. Known by heart, it's company. It comes back on its own while you're driving or washing up, and each time you understand a little more. You don't need a whole bani to start. Two lines, really known, are enough to be there when you need them.
screen: `KANTH: KEPT IN THE THROAT.` · `GURBANI CARRIED IN MEMORY.` · `THE BANI IS LIGHT IN THE MIND.` · `TWO LINES, REALLY KNOWN.` · then, large: `BY HEART.`

Do the same with the second, then say both together; if you lose a word, peek and try again, no rush. If you pray, let the lines be your prayer.

679.title: Singing it for someone
679.hook: a shabad sung for a sick or grieving friend is a gift
679.howItsDone: When someone is ill or has died, Sikh families and friends often gather at home for Sukhmani Sahib, kirtan and Ardas, singing shabads of comfort for the person and the family.

segments.voice: Yesterday, kanth, and your line: by heart. That closes a week that made the forest at home, sang laments, honored the brave, kept a shabad for the house, chose the right song and learned it by heart. Today: give it away.
screen: `THE FOREST AT HOME · ALL MUST GO · ACCEPTED · OUR SHABAD · THE RIGHT SONG · BY HEART.`

segments.voice: What do you say to a friend whose father just died? What do you bring to a hospital room? Flowers wilt, food piles up, and words come out wrong. Even a kind text can feel thin. Some Sikh families have an old answer. They sit by the bed, or in the living room of the grieving house, and they sing. Not performers: aunties, cousins, a neighbor with a harmonium. Today: singing it for someone.
screen: `WHAT DO YOU SAY?` → `FLOWERS WILT, WORDS COME OUT WRONG.` → `SO THEY SING.`

segments.voice: In Sikh life, a shabad can be a gift you give with your voice. When someone is ill, families often gather for a reading of Sukhmani Sahib, the Psalm of Peace, or for kirtan at home, and end with an Ardas asking for the person's wellbeing. When someone has died, the sangat gathers at the family's house in the days that follow, for readings and kirtan, so the family isn't alone with the silence. What gets sung? Often a shabad of comfort. One line turned to in illness comes from Sukhmani Sahib, on Ang two seventy-four. In paraphrase: the Name is the medicine for every illness. Others sing the hot wind that doesn't touch, or the Name that destroys pain. Why singing, and not just talking? Sikhs give a few reasons. The words aren't yours: you don't have to find the perfect thing to say, because the Guru has already said it. Singing is shared: the sick person can listen with their eyes closed, and nobody has to make conversation. And it carries something beyond the singer. Sikhs understand the shabad as the Guru's own voice, so singing it for someone offers them the Guru's company, not just yours. The quiet part: it doesn't have to be good. A wobbly voice, a phone playing a recording, a line whispered at a bedside. The gift is the attention, and the Word.
screen: `A GIFT GIVEN WITH YOUR VOICE.` · `SUKHMANI AND KIRTAN AT HOME.` · `THE NAME, MEDICINE FOR ILLNESS.` · `IT DOESN'T HAVE TO BE GOOD.` · then, large: `SING IT FOR THEM.`

segments.voice: Think of someone who's sick, tired or grieving right now, and picture their face. Take your two lines from yesterday, or any line you love, and say or hum them softly, as if for that person, without worrying how it sounds. If you pray, you can say Waheguru for them.
Aukhad, medicine: a shabad given to a sick or grieving friend is medicine too, the Guru's words offered with your own voice, however it sounds.
Your line: sing it for them. The words are already written. Day six hundred seventy-nine, done.
